notes: Original short, human-curated, read-only procedures. General steps are labelled as general investigation methods. Official procedures reference an existing approved KB card. No live system actions or auto-execution.

playbooks.title: Put the failures and changes on one timeline
playbooks.summary: See what began first, whether the symptoms overlap and whether a deployment is a credible lead.
playbooks.applies_when: Several symptoms or a recent change could be related. No particular vendor is required.

steps.instruction: Collect the first and last known timestamps for each symptom, and the deployment or configuration-change time. Record the time zone for every source.
Use existing incident dashboards, audit events and application logs to compare the same time window. Avoid changing monitoring settings just to run the check.
Note whether the symptoms consistently occur together, and whether one tends to appear before another.
Look for periods when a symptom occurs alone. Those exceptions are just as useful as overlaps.

interpretation.supports: A repeated sequence, such as database delays first and then checkout errors, strengthens the case for a shared dependency.
interpretation.weakens: If the symptoms occur at different times or started well before the change, that weakens a single-cause explanation.
interpretation.unknown: Matching timestamps suggest a connection, but timing on its own cannot prove causation.

playbooks.share_back: Tell Scout the earliest timestamp of each symptom and when the change was deployed.

playbooks.title: Check whether the affected services share a dependency
playbooks.summary: Find out if the failing customer journey, API and database actually rely on the same components.
playbooks.applies_when: Multiple services could be experiencing the same underlying fault.

steps.instruction: Sketch the simplest route a failed request takes: user -> gateway -> application/API -> database or downstream service, using your organisation's diagrams where available.
Identify which database, pool, queue, network service or external API each affected component uses. Mark anything shared.
Compare one failing request with one successful request to see whether they pass through the same dependencies.
Do not conclude that services are linked just because their errors sound alike; look for an actual shared component.

interpretation.supports: If all affected requests stall at the same dependency, prioritise evidence from that component.
interpretation.weakens: If the failing paths do not share the suspected dependency, look for another explanation.
interpretation.unknown: A shared component makes a connection possible; it does not show the component is faulty.

playbooks.share_back: Tell Scout which systems share the same database or service, and which ones do not.

playbooks.title: Follow one failed request from start to finish
playbooks.summary: Locate the first delay or failure rather than assuming the database or gateway is at fault.
playbooks.applies_when: There is an API, request, customer transaction or multi-service process to follow.

steps.instruction: Choose one failed request or checkout attempt and note its time, endpoint and correlation/request/trace ID if available. Don't enter real customer details into Scout.
Find the request in the gateway or API logs, then follow the same ID through any application, database-call or downstream-service traces already collected.
Compare timestamps and durations at each hop. Identify where response time first increases or where an error is first logged.
Repeat with a successful request around the same time to compare the differences.

interpretation.supports: If the delay begins at database calls across failed traces, database-side investigation becomes a stronger next step.
interpretation.weakens: If requests are slow before they reach the database, a database-first explanation becomes less likely.
interpretation.unknown: Without request IDs or end-to-end traces, use timestamp correlation and report that limitation.

playbooks.share_back: Tell Scout which part of the request first slowed down, and how the successful request differed.

playbooks.title: Investigate an HTTP 504 gateway timeout
playbooks.summary: Compare gateway timeouts with upstream response times using matching request timestamps.
playbooks.applies_when: Only when the error is actually an HTTP 504 returned by a gateway or reverse proxy.

steps.instruction: Record the exact HTTP status (504), affected endpoint, time, and whether the problem is intermittent or consistent.
Check gateway or reverse-proxy access/error logs at that time, noting the upstream destination and measured duration if your logging system records them.
Check the corresponding upstream application logs or monitoring for delayed responses, resource pressure or connection problems.
Compare with a successful request and the configured timeout if available. Do not increase timeouts until the underlying delay is understood.

interpretation.supports: A gateway timeout paired with a slow upstream response supports investigating the upstream delay.
interpretation.weakens: If the upstream responds promptly but the gateway still times out, examine the proxy's connection path and its logs.
interpretation.unknown: A 504 says the gateway waited too long. It does not prove the database, network or application is the root cause.

playbooks.share_back: Tell Scout the 504 timestamp and whether the upstream application logged a matching slow request.

playbooks.title: Inspect PostgreSQL sessions and waits
playbooks.summary: Use a documented read-only statistics view to see active sessions and waiting work.
playbooks.applies_when: Only if the user has said the affected database is PostgreSQL and the investigating engineer has read access.

steps.instruction: Connect with an authorised read-only database account. Do not share credentials or sensitive query text with Scout.
Run this SELECT query in an approved SQL client to count client sessions by state and wait type. It reads pg_stat_activity; it does not change data.
steps.command:
SELECT datname, state, wait_event_type, wait_event,
       COUNT(*) AS sessions
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'
GROUP BY datname, state, wait_event_type, wait_event
ORDER BY sessions DESC;

steps.instruction: Compare the result with your normal baseline and the affected time window. A current snapshot may miss an earlier spike.
If you need to understand storage or server memory, use separate approved host or database monitoring. pg_stat_activity does not report free memory or disk space.

interpretation.supports: An unusually high session count, long-running activity or repeated waits during the fault may support a contention or saturation hypothesis.
interpretation.weakens: Normal session levels and no relevant waits during the fault weaken that particular explanation, but do not exclude other database issues.
interpretation.unknown: Seeing waits does not automatically identify the blocking process or prove it caused the customer failures. Visibility can depend on database permissions.

playbooks.share_back: Tell Scout whether session counts or waits rose during the incident, without pasting sensitive query text.

playbooks.title: Check why a Kubernetes Pod is restarting
playbooks.summary: Review Pod events and earlier container logs before proposing any changes.
playbooks.applies_when: Only if the affected workload runs in Kubernetes and the user has read-only kubectl access.

steps.instruction: Confirm the Pod name and namespace using the cluster's normal tooling. Use the placeholders below only after replacing them with real names.
Inspect the Pod's events, restart count, readiness and the last termination reason.
Inspect the previous instance's logs if the container has restarted.
Compare the restart time with recent deployments, memory-limit events and health probe failures. Do not disable probes or restart workloads as an initial diagnostic step.

interpretation.supports: A recorded OOM kill, probe failure or application exception provides a more specific lead to test.
interpretation.weakens: If restarts predate the deployment or no relevant change occurred, the deployment explanation is less likely.
interpretation.unknown: A restart reason helps locate the failure, but it may still be a symptom of another dependency.

playbooks.share_back: Tell Scout the Pod's last termination reason, restart count and any matching event, without copying credentials or secrets.
